name: VASP Software GmbH (Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package)
origin_detail: Based on Mike Payne's MIT code (also the root of CASTEP), brought to the University of Vienna by Jurgen Hafner in July 1989; the main program was written by Jurgen Furthmuller (from 1993) and Georg Kresse, who still leads development. Licences were historically agreements with the University of Vienna; VASP Software GmbH in Vienna is now the copyright holder and licensor, with Materials Design Inc. as exclusive distributor to commercial users.
openness_notes: Proprietary. Source code is delivered to licensed research groups through the VASP Portal but is confidential under the licence agreement and never public. Licences go to one named research group at one site (not departments or individuals), for non-profit research only; a VASP.5.4.4 group licence capped named users at six. In June 2026 the company issued AI-tool guidelines forbidding licensees from feeding VASP source or the PP database to public/consumer AI models or using the code to train AI models or build a VASP equivalent.

risk_events: 2026: licence enforcement tightened; HPC centres report a switch from group-based checks to personal licence-key validation (VASP 6.6.1 already; 6.5.1 from 1 Oct 2026).
16 Jun 2026: guidelines restrict AI coding tools on VASP source, reflecting the risk that LLMs could clone the code.
Jul 2026: serious force bug in VASP 6.6.0 (spin-polarized meta-GGA) required an urgent 6.6.1 patch; groups whose licence did not cover 6.6.1 had to apply a patch file.
robustness: Commercially self-sustaining for ~35 years with a single development centre in Vienna (Kresse group). Users cannot fork or redistribute; continuity depends on the company and its licence terms. Open alternatives (Quantum ESPRESSO, ABINIT) exist but VASP results and PAW datasets underpin much published and database work.
physical_science_relevance: A dominant DFT code in materials science; most large computed-materials databases (including the Materials Project) were generated with VASP, so open data downstream rests on a closed upstream engine.
openness_effect_assessment: Staying closed lets VASP fund a dedicated developer team from licence fees rather than grants, and it remains a reference code with more than 1,400 licensed research groups. The cost is restricted reproducibility and reuse: groups cannot share the code, and in 2026 the vendor moved to prevent AI tools from ingesting it. Its outputs nonetheless flow into open databases such as the Materials Project.
key_takeaway: VASP is the clearest closed counterpoint in physical-science software: an academic code that commercialised through group licences, kept source confidential, and in 2026 explicitly barred AI training on its code. It shows that closed scientific software can be long-lived and high-impact, while open data built on its outputs (Materials Project) ended up becoming the AI training resource.
